cards.front: The **four drivers** of the ERP revolution (mnemonic?)
cards.back:
**EPIC** — each is a *from → to* shift:
**E** — from department → **Enterprise**
**P** — from function → **Process**
**I** — from information silos → **Integrated** information system
**C** — from departmental DBs → one **Common** database

*Marks are lost for giving only the destination — always say "from X to Y".*

cards.front: The **six ERP life-cycle phases** in order (mnemonic?)
cards.back:
**Papa Please Bring Rice For Supper**
1. **P**re-Implementation *(Evaluation)*
2. **P**roject Preparation
3. **B**usiness Blueprinting *(Design)*
4. **R**ealization *(Build)*
5. **F**inal Preparation & Go Live
6. **S**upport *(Manage / Sustain)*

**ERP Lifecycle = Implementation Life cycle + Support Life cycle**

**SPACES**
**S** — SCM (Supply Chain Management)
**P** — PLM (Product Lifecycle Management)
**A** — APS (Advanced Planning and Scheduling)
**C** — CRM (Customer Relationship Management)
**E** — EAM (Enterprise Asset Management)
**S** — SRM (Supplier Relationship Management)

**DNS**
**D** — **Duplication** of data
**N** — **No integration** between departmental databases
**S** — **Systems** not able to update all relevant information online

*Stated question-bank answer with an exact count — three.*

cards.front: The **four tangible / direct benefits** of ERP (mnemonic?)
cards.back:
**I-C-O-M** — *"I COMe out ahead"*
**I** — **Inventory** reduction
**C** — Better **Customer** service & reduced lost sales
**O** — Reducing days **Outstanding**
**M** — **Material and labour** cost reduction

*Three of the four release **working capital** — ERP's financial case is largely a working-capital case.*

**DUKE**
**D** — Don't start a project with a **Deadline** in mind
**U** — **Update** your budget projection at regular intervals
**E** — **ERP isn't only about the software**
**K** — **Keep** the communication lines open

*Jeri Dunn: "No major software implementation is really about the software."*

**I See People (I-S-P)**
**I** — **Implementation** challenges *(6 items)*
**S** — **Support / maintenance** challenges *(6 items)*
**P** — Managing **People** challenges *(4 items)*

*They map onto the life cycle: I = phases 1–5, S = phase 6, P = all of them.*

cards.front: The **four deployment strategies** as a grid
cards.back:
A **2 × 2** of *locations* × *modules*:

| | **All modules** | **Selected modules** |
|---|---|---|
| **All locations** | **Big Bang** | **Big Bang Modular** |
| **Selected locations** | **Rollout** | **Rollout Modular** |

**Big Bang** = all locations · **Rollout** = selected locations · **Modular** = selected modules

**Risk and Time move in opposite directions:**
- **Big Bang** — high risk, **low time**
- **Rollout** — average / average
- **Big Bang Modular** — high risk, average time
- **Rollout Modular** — **low risk**, high time

**Learning scope is the reversed row** — *High is good*, and Big Bang is **Low** because there is no "later" to learn into.

cards.front: The **evolution ladder** and what each step adds
cards.back:
**MRP** *(1960–70s)* — materials only
**Closed-loop MRP** — + **capacity / feasibility check**
**MRP II** *(1980s)* — + **accounting & billing**, forecasting, S&OP
**ERP** *(1990s)* — + **every other function**; non-manufacturing too
**Extended ERP / ERP II** *(2000s)* — + **suppliers & customers** (outside the company)

cards.front: **MRP vs Closed-loop MRP** — the exact difference
cards.back:
**MRP does not consider the capacity available while planning**, so its plan may be infeasible — it assumes **infinite capacity**.

**Closed-loop MRP** validates the plan, **compares it with reality, checks feasibility**, and reports **alerts and triggers** to the planner.

*One line: MRP plans as if capacity were unlimited; closed-loop MRP checks it.*

**ERP is an integrated information system built on a centralized database and having a common computing platform that helps in effective usage of enterprise's resources and facilitates the flow of information between all business functions of the enterprise (and with external stakeholders).**

*Five mark-bearing phrases — and don't drop the last clause.*

**Enterprise** — an organization providing products/services to society; a business entity *(Airtel, Tatas, Reliance, IBM, Google, Apple)*
**Resource** — human resource, machines, plants, storehouses, material stock
**Planning** — production, forecasts, money, new products, logistics, maintenance

**P2P** — Procure to Pay
**O2C** — Quote / Order to Cash
**F2S** — Forecast to Stock
**T2M** — Time to Market
**H2R** — Hire to Retire
**F2F** — Farm to Fork

*Every name states its own start and end. **P2P is money out; O2C is money in.***

cards.front: The **seven stages of Quote to Cash**
cards.back:
1. **Quote / Proposal** → Sales Quote
2. **Quote Approval** *(by the customer)* → Approved Quote
3. **Sales Order** → Sales Order
4. **Fulfillment / Delivery** → Goods Delivered
5. **Invoicing** → Customer Invoice
6. **Payment Receipt** → Payment Received
7. **Cash Application** → Cash Applied / Account Closed

*It does not end at delivery — stages 5–7 are about getting paid.*

cards.front: The **four ERP implementation types** and the trade-off
cards.back:
**On-premises · Cloud · Hybrid · Two-tier**

Two pure types + two mixtures — **Hybrid mixes by *module*, Two-tier mixes by *location*.**

**Control ↑ ⇒ Cost ↑, Flexibility ↓**
- On-prem: High / High / **Low**
- Cloud: Low / Low / High
- Hybrid: Medium / Medium / High
- Two-tier: Central+Local / Medium / High

cards.front: The **four branded methodologies** and their owners
cards.back:
**ASAP** → **SAP** *(Accelerated SAP)*
**Ascendant** → **PwC / IBM**
**AIM / Fast Forward** → **Oracle**
**Signature** → **Scala / Epicor**

*Nestlé used SAP; Agilent used Oracle.*

**Objectives** — *"Quick Managers Involve Process Reuse"*: Quick & cost effective · Maximize resource utilization · Involve users community · Process oriented · Re-usability

**Tools:** Roadmap composer · Q&A database · **Project IMG** (Implementation Guide) · **Transports** (config dev→deployment) · **BC Sets** (configuration recorder)

**As-Is** + **To-Be** ⇒ **Gap**

Deliverables: **Current model (As-Is) · Detailed requirement · Gap document · Future To-Be process**

*The **gap document** is where the project's real cost is decided — every gap must be **customized** or **absorbed by changing the business**. Gap analysis is "the most important step of ERP implementation".*

**Configuration** — setting options the package already provides. Low risk, survives upgrades.
**Customization** — **code-level changes** to the base package. High risk.

**Customization risks:** **stability** of base functionality · **deviating from best practice** · **maintainability**

*Customize heavily and you forfeit "brings best practices" — the main benefit you paid for.*

- **10% of ERP implementations succeed**
- **Cost overruns average 178%** *(≈ 2.78× budget)*
- **Schedule overruns average 230%** *(≈ 3.3× schedule)*
- **Implemented functionality averages 41%** of what is desired

*Another survey: **51% of implementers felt unsuccessful**.*

1. **Identify** risks
2. **Analyze impact**
3. **Assess probability**
4. **Prioritize**
5. **Mitigation** plan creation
6. **Contingency** plan creation

**Mitigation acts *before* (reduce probability/impact); contingency acts *after* (cope if it happens).** Parallel runs = mitigation; cut-over contingency plans = contingency.

**Test: does an invoice arrive?**

**Direct (9):** Hardware · OS & DB · Application licence · Application maintenance (AMC) · Complimentary software · Consulting · Post-implementation support · Training · PMO
*Buckets: **Iron, Software, People, Overhead***

**Indirect (2) — "People and Pause":** Internal employee cost · Operational disruption cost *(+ opportunity costs)*

**Grand total 1,914 lakhs** over 5–6 years.
Top three: **Consulting 800 · AMC 280 · Licence 269** = **70%** — and **none of them is hardware**.

**AMC (280) exceeds the licence fee (269)** — owning outgrows buying.

**Cash flow: Year 1 = 1,294 (68% of total)**, then ~122/yr. **Costs peak in Year 1; benefits peak from Year 3.**

cards.front: The worked **business case** — the 23.62 Cr computation
cards.back:
Company with **2,000 Cr turnover**, ERP cost **19.14 Cr**:
- **Labour** 2% of 200 Cr → **4 Cr**
- **Material** 1% of 1000 Cr → **1 Cr**
- **Inventory turnover 5 → 6**: 400 Cr → 333 Cr, reduction **67 Cr**, @12% → **8 Cr**
- **Debtors** (50 → 45 days): working capital 68.4 → 54.79, 13.6 @12% → **1.62 Cr**

**Total = 23.62 Crore per year.**

1. *"ERP is just a computer software system"* — it is **much beyond h/w, s/w & network**
2. *"ERP is only for manufacturing"* — due to its **MRP → MRP II → ERP** origins
3. *"ERP can automate all operations"* — it moves **data/information**, not material or actual work
4. *"ERP is ready-made and deploys quickly"* — needs **customization, expert consultancy, management commitment**

**Production → Quantity** *(large batches, standardized, fewer variations — lowers setup time and cost)*
**Sales → Variety** *(colours, sizes, models — attracts more customers)*

**Both are doing their jobs correctly; their objectives are simply opposite.** Classic **local optimization defeating global optimization**.

*Pizza version: the kitchen wants one type; customers want four.*

**Multi-** Division/Product · Location/Facilities · Country · Currency · Lingual · Cultural · **(mixed) mode manufacturing** — plus **24 × 7 × 365 operations**

*Expanding sequence: grow products → divisions; grow beyond a city → locations; **cross a border and currency, language and culture come free**.*

cards.front: **Porter's Value Chain** — primary and support activities
cards.back:
**Primary — "In → Make → Out → Sell → Serve":** Inbound logistics · Operations · Outbound logistics · Marketing & Sales · Service

**Support:** Firm infrastructure · Human Resource Management · Technology development · **Procurement**

*Each activity adds value; worked together, **total value > total cost = margin**. Note Procurement is a **support** activity here, though P2P is a core ERP process.*

Project **BEST**, **SAP** + Manugistics, **1997–2001**, **$210M** budget.

**Problem:** **29 different prices for vanilla to the same vendor**; **9 general ledgers, 28 points of customer entry**.

**What happened:** confusion → resistance → **rebellion in 2000**; reconstructed June 2000.

**Outcome:** forecast accuracy **+2%**, **$371 million saved by 2001**.

**Project Everest**, **Oracle E-Business Suite**, **2000–2004**, **$220M**, ~100 Oracle consultants. Migrating **2,200 legacy applications** from HP.

**Damage:** **$88M** reduction in Q3 orders (**$38M lost**, $50M delayed); **$105M lost revenue**, **$70M operating profit**; extra **$35M** costs. Cause: **backlog conversion** for highly configured products.

**Lesson:** *"ERP disasters are often caused by a user company itself."*

**Introduction → Growth → Maturity → Decline** *(Revenue and Profit vs Time)*

**Profit lags revenue and peaks earlier** — negative in Introduction, and already falling in Maturity while revenue is still at its peak.

*Implication: start the **next** product during **Maturity**, while the current one still funds it. Shortening **T2M** shifts the whole curve left.*

cards.front: ERP **market structure** and the top players
cards.back:
**"Stratification of products — SAP, Oracle & the rest."**

**SAP and Oracle** are the Tier-1 leaders; then **Microsoft (Dynamics)**, **Infor**, IFS, Epicor, Sage Intacct, Acumatica, Odoo, Unit4, QAD.

*The top concentrates while the bottom opens to SMEs — **the middle (niche players) gets squeezed**.*

Sorted by *what already exists*:
- **Nothing** → **First-time implementation**
- **Same ERP, old** → **Upgrade** *(obsolescence / new functionality)*
- **Same ERP, only here** → **Global roll-out** *(global template + country enhancements)*
- **A different ERP** → **Migration** *(unhappy, or no longer supported)*
- **Too many ERPs** → **Harmonization / Consolidation**
- **It works** → **Support / Sustain**

**Ten final checks**, ending with **Go / No-Go** *(everything before it is evidence; the switchover can still be refused)*.

**At cut-over:** switch over · **execute parallel runs of the old system for a defined period** · Help Desk & hand-holding · **typically done in phases/batches** · fine-tune configuration.

*Parallel run = insurance: it's how you **detect** a wrong number and how the business survives a failure.*

**Pre-Implementation** happens **before commitment** — ends with package & partner selected, **budget approved, contracts signed**. The org could still say no.

**Project Preparation** happens **after commitment** — detailed plan, **project charter**, methodology, solution architecture, hardware sizing.

***Phase 1 chooses whether and with whom; Phase 2 chooses how.***
